10720:
To miscalculate means to make an error in working something out — whether that "something" is a number, a distance, a cost, or even a real-life situation.

Think of it in two parts:

  • "mis-" = wrongly, badly, incorrectly
  • "calculate" = to figure out, to work out, to assess

Put them together, and you get: to figure something out incorrectly.
Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. With numbers, amounts, or measurements (the literal use)

This is the most direct use. When you do a calculation — addition, subtraction, measurements, costs, distances — and you get the wrong answer, you have miscalculated.

Examples:

  • The engineer miscalculated the weight the bridge could hold, so it was not safe.
  • She miscalculated the ingredients for the recipe and added too much salt.
  • The accountant miscalculated the taxes, so the company paid less than it should have.
  • I miscalculated how long it would take to walk to the station and missed my train.

In each of these, someone ran numbers or estimates through their mind (or on paper) and arrived at a wrong result.

2. With situations, people, or decisions (the figurative use — and equally important)

This is where miscalculate truly stretches its wings. In everyday language, people use it to mean misjudging a situation, underestimating or overestimating something, or making a wrong assessment of how events will unfold.

You don't need numbers for this. What you do need is a prediction, a plan, or a judgment — and then getting it badly wrong.

Examples:

  • The politician miscalculated the public's mood and lost the election badly. (He thought people would support him; they didn't.)
  • The company miscalculated how popular the new product would be and made far too many of them.
  • She miscalculated his reaction — she thought he would be upset, but he was actually relieved.
  • The general miscalculated the enemy's strength and led his army into a trap.
  • He miscalculated when he thought his boss wouldn't notice the missing report.

In all these cases, someone formed a mental estimate or judgment about reality — and that estimate turned out to be wrong in a meaningful way that had real consequences.
The Key Idea Behind Both Uses

Whether it involves numbers or judgment, the heart of "miscalculate" is this:

You applied your mind to figure something out. You thought you had the right answer. But you were wrong — and that wrongness had a consequence.

This is why miscalculate feels stronger than simply "making a mistake." It implies that there was a process of reasoning involved — you weren't randomly guessing; you were thinking it through — but your thinking led you astray.

• It does not mean you were lazy or careless (though that can cause a miscalculation). Someone who works very hard and still gets the wrong answer has still miscalculated.
  • It does not mean a random accident. If a vase falls off a shelf by itself, that's not a miscalculation. But if you misjudged whether the vase was stable and placed it on the edge — and it fell — that is a miscalculation.
  • It is not the same as lying. A person who miscalculates genuinely believed their estimate or calculation was right.

Miscalculations can be small or enormous:

  • Small: "I miscalculated how much coffee to make — I made too much."
  • Large: "The government miscalculated the consequences of its policy, causing a financial crisis."

The word fits both. What scales with the severity is not the word itself, but the context around it. This makes "miscalculate" a very flexible and powerful word.

Miscalculate carries a tone of serious error with consequences. It is not a casual word. When someone says "I miscalculated," it usually signals that:

  1. They were confident in their assessment beforehand.
  2. Reality did not match what they expected.
  3. There was some kind of cost — financial, social, political, or practical.

It often appears in contexts of strategy, planning, politics, business, and engineering — anywhere that careful thinking is expected and mistakes carry a price.
Verb Forms (How to Use It in Sentences)

FormExample
miscalculate (base/infinitive)"It's easy to miscalculate the risks."
miscalculates (present, 3rd person)"He often miscalculates people's intentions."
miscalculated (past tense)"They miscalculated the cost of the project."
miscalculating (present participle)"She realized she was miscalculating the distance."

Miscalculation (noun) — the act of miscalculating, or the error itself.

  • "The bridge collapse was the result of a serious miscalculation."
  • "His miscalculation cost the team the championship."
To miscalculate is to work something out wrongly in your mind — whether it is a number, a cost, a distance, or a real-life situation — often with consequences you did not expect.
10721:
A miscarriage of justice is when the legal system produces a deeply wrong or unfair outcome — most commonly, when an innocent person is convicted and punished for a crime they did not commit.

Think of it this way: Justice is supposed to be a fair, accurate machine. A miscarriage of justice is when that machine breaks down and spits out the wrong result.
Breaking Down the Words

The word "miscarriage" doesn't just mean a pregnancy loss in medical terms. In its broader, older meaning, it means a failure or something going badly wrong. When a plan "miscarries," it fails completely.

So "miscarriage of justice" literally means: justice has failed. The system that was supposed to protect people and find the truth has instead produced a result that is wrong, harmful, or deeply unfair.
The Core Meaning — Expanded

When a criminal justice system works correctly, it:

  • Investigates a crime properly
  • Gathers accurate evidence
  • Gives the accused a fair trial
  • Convicts only the guilty
  • Punishes proportionately

A miscarriage of justice happens when any part of this process goes so badly wrong that the final outcome is a serious injustice. The term is most powerfully — and most commonly — used when an innocent person is found guilty and punished for something they didn't do. That is its most recognized and most devastating form.

However, the term is also used in other situations where justice has clearly failed, which we'll cover below.
The Different Forms a Miscarriage of Justice Can Take

1. Wrongful Conviction (The Most Common and Serious Form)

This is when an innocent person is found guilty by a court and is sentenced — perhaps to prison, or in extreme cases, even to death. The person loses their freedom, reputation, and years of their life for something they never did. This is the form most people mean when they use the phrase "miscarriage of justice."

2. Wrongful Acquittal

This is when a person who is actually guilty of a serious crime is found not guilty and walks free. While courts prefer to err on the side of innocence (and rightly so), if a guilty person escapes justice because of corrupt procedures, suppressed evidence, or a flawed process — rather than genuine reasonable doubt — this too can be considered a miscarriage of justice.

3. Grossly Disproportionate Sentencing

Sometimes the right person is convicted of the right crime, but the punishment handed down is wildly excessive or shockingly lenient compared to what the law and the circumstances demand. This imbalance can itself be a miscarriage of justice.

4. Procedural Failures That Corrupt the Outcome

If a person didn't receive a fair trial — for example, they were denied proper legal representation, the jury was tampered with, or a judge was biased — the entire process is tainted. Even if the person happened to be guilty, the corrupted process is itself a miscarriage of justice because the result cannot be trusted.
What Causes a Miscarriage of Justice?

Understanding the causes is crucial, because miscarriages of justice don't usually happen because someone just got unlucky. They happen because of specific, identifiable failures. Here are the most common:

False Confessions

It sounds unbelievable, but innocent people sometimes confess to crimes they didn't commit. This can happen because of extreme psychological pressure during police interrogations, fear, mental illness, exhaustion, or coercive tactics by investigators who are convinced they have the right person.

Eyewitness Misidentification

Human memory is far less reliable than most people think. A witness who genuinely and sincerely believes they saw someone commit a crime can be completely wrong. Studies have shown that eyewitness misidentification is one of the single biggest causes of wrongful convictions. Factors like stress, poor lighting, racial cross-identification bias, and the passage of time all make eyewitness testimony unreliable — yet courts and juries tend to trust it heavily.

Flawed or Fabricated Forensic Evidence

Sometimes scientific evidence presented in court is later proven to be faulty, outdated, or even fabricated. In past decades, certain forensic techniques that seemed reliable — like bite-mark analysis, hair comparison, and some fire investigation methods — have been shown by modern science to lack the accuracy that was once claimed for them. In worse cases, forensic experts have deliberately falsified results.

Police Misconduct

Some miscarriages of justice result from officers who are either corrupt, overzealous, or under pressure to close a case. They might plant evidence, coerce witnesses, hide information that points to the suspect's innocence, or selectively pursue only the suspect they've already decided is guilty — ignoring leads that might point elsewhere.

Prosecutorial Misconduct

Prosecutors are supposed to seek justice — not just win cases. But some prosecutors suppress exculpatory evidence (evidence that could prove innocence), rely on witnesses they know are unreliable, or make misleading arguments to the jury. This is one of the most serious breaches of legal ethics and a significant cause of wrongful convictions.

Inadequate Legal Defense

In many countries, people who cannot afford a lawyer are provided one by the state. These public defenders are often overworked, underfunded, and unable to give every case the attention it needs. A defendant with a poor legal defense is far more vulnerable to a wrongful conviction, even if there are obvious problems with the prosecution's case.

Tunnel Vision

This is a psychological trap where investigators, prosecutors, or even judges become so convinced that a particular person is guilty that they stop looking at the evidence objectively. Anything that supports guilt is emphasized; anything that points to innocence is dismissed or ignored. The entire investigation becomes about building a case against one person, rather than finding the truth.

Perjury (Lying Under Oath)

Witnesses — including sometimes informants who receive benefits in exchange for their testimony — may lie in court. A false witness statement can be devastatingly persuasive to a jury, especially when there is little other evidence.

Racial, Social, and Economic Bias

Justice systems are run by human beings, and human beings carry biases — sometimes conscious, often unconscious. People from marginalized communities, those who are poor, or those who face racial prejudice may receive less thorough investigations on their behalf, less credibility from juries, and less vigorous legal defenses. These systemic inequalities make miscarriages of justice more likely for certain groups.
A Real-World Example to Make It Concrete

Imagine a man named Thomas. A convenience store is robbed at gunpoint. A witness sees a man running nearby and tells police. Under pressure, she identifies Thomas in a photo lineup — but she's not fully certain. The police, already suspecting Thomas for unrelated reasons, focus entirely on him. They don't follow up on other leads. A forensic analyst overstates the significance of fibers found at the scene. Thomas can't afford a top lawyer. At trial, the jury hears the witness's identification, the forensic testimony, and convicts Thomas. He is sentenced to 15 years in prison.

Ten years later, DNA evidence that was never tested at trial is re-examined and conclusively points to someone else. Thomas is exonerated — released and formally declared innocent. But by then, he has lost a decade of his life, his career, his family relationships, and his health. He walked into prison innocent and walked out with nothing to show for it but years stolen from him.

That is a miscarriage of justice — every step of that process, from the tunnel-visioned investigation to the unreliable testimony to the flawed forensic evidence, combined to destroy an innocent man's life.
The Consequences for the Victim

A miscarriage of justice inflicts a profound and multi-layered harm on the wrongly convicted person:

Loss of freedom — They spend months, years, or even decades imprisoned for something they didn't do.

Damaged reputation — Even after exoneration, the stigma of having been convicted of a serious crime can follow a person. Friends, family, employers, and communities may never fully trust them again.

Psychological trauma — The experience of being disbelieved, convicted, imprisoned, and stripped of agency causes severe psychological damage, including PTSD, depression, and anxiety.

Financial devastation — Lost income, legal costs, and the near-impossibility of rebuilding a career after wrongful imprisonment can leave exonerees in severe poverty.

Broken relationships — Time in prison destroys marriages, separates parents from children, and severs friendships.

Lost years — Perhaps most painfully of all, time cannot be recovered. Years of a person's life — their youth, their health, moments with loved ones — are simply gone.
How Are Miscarriages of Justice Discovered and Corrected?

Appeals

After a conviction, a defendant has the right to appeal — to ask a higher court to review whether the trial was conducted fairly and legally. An appeal is not a second trial; it typically examines whether errors of law or procedure occurred that may have affected the outcome. If a serious error is found, the conviction may be quashed (overturned).

Post-Conviction Review

In many justice systems, there are formal bodies specifically tasked with reviewing cases where a miscarriage of justice may have occurred. In the UK, for example, the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) investigates potential miscarriages and can refer cases back to the Court of Appeal.

New Evidence

Sometimes new evidence emerges after a conviction — a new witness comes forward, someone confesses, or previously untested evidence is analyzed. The most famous modern example is DNA evidence, which has revolutionized the ability to re-examine old cases. Organizations like the Innocence Project in the United States have used DNA testing to exonerate hundreds of wrongly convicted people.

Media Investigation and Public Pressure

Journalists, documentarians, and campaigners sometimes take up cases they believe represent a wrongful conviction and bring them to public attention. This external scrutiny can force legal authorities to re-examine cases they would otherwise leave closed.

Pardons

A head of state or government authority may grant a pardon to someone wrongly convicted. However, a pardon is not the same as an exoneration — it forgives the offense but doesn't officially declare the person innocent. A full exoneration (a formal, legal declaration of innocence) is a more meaningful remedy.
The Difference Between Key Related Terms

Since you're learning, it helps to understand how this term relates to similar words:

Wrongful conviction — Essentially the same as a miscarriage of justice in its most common sense, but slightly more specific. It refers specifically to the act of convicting an innocent person. "Miscarriage of justice" is the broader umbrella term for any profound failure of the justice system.

Exoneration — This is what happens after a miscarriage of justice is proven. To exonerate someone means to officially clear them of blame or guilt. It is the remedy, not the problem.

Unsafe conviction — A legal term used particularly in UK law. A conviction is called "unsafe" when there is reason to believe it may be unreliable — perhaps because of new evidence, procedural errors, or concerns about how the evidence was presented. An unsafe conviction doesn't necessarily mean the person is innocent; it means the conviction cannot be confidently trusted.

Acquittal — When someone is found not guilty at trial. This is different from exoneration; an acquittal just means the prosecution didn't prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The person may still be widely believed to be guilty.
Why Miscarriages of Justice Matter Beyond the Individual

A miscarriage of justice doesn't just harm the individual. It damages the entire concept of justice itself in several important ways:

The real criminal goes free. When an innocent person is convicted, the actual guilty party is out in society — unpunished, and often free to commit more crimes.

Public trust is eroded. When people see innocent individuals imprisoned by a system that is supposed to protect them, trust in police, courts, and the law collapses. This erosion of trust makes it harder for law enforcement to do its job.

It exposes systemic failures. Each miscarriage of justice is a warning sign of deeper problems — whether in policing, prosecution, forensic science, or legal aid — that need to be fixed to prevent future injustices.

It raises moral questions about punishment. If a system can get it this wrong, it forces society to ask: are our punishments too severe? Should we have the death penalty if we can't be certain of guilt? These are among the most profound questions in law and ethics.
The Phrase in Everyday Use

While the term has a precise legal meaning, people also use "miscarriage of justice" more loosely in everyday conversation to describe any situation where fairness has been badly violated — for instance, when someone loses their job unfairly, or when a decision-maker ignores clear evidence. However, in its proper, formal sense, it always refers to a failure of the legal or judicial system.
Summary

AspectWhat You Need to Know

A miscarriage of justice is a profound failure of the legal system to deliver a fair, accurate, and just outcome. At its most serious, it means an innocent person is convicted and punished for a crime they didn't commit. It can also describe other major failures — such as a guilty person escaping justice through a corrupted process, or a wildly disproportionate sentence. It is caused by a combination of human failures: false confessions, unreliable eyewitnesses, bad forensic evidence, police misconduct, prosecutorial misconduct, poor legal defense, tunnel vision, and systemic bias. It is discovered through appeals, new evidence (especially DNA), independent review bodies, and journalism. It is corrected through quashed convictions, exonerations, and pardons — but the harm done to the wrongly convicted person can never be fully undone. It matters not just because of what it does to the individual, but because it undermines the entire foundation of what a justice system is supposed to stand for: the truth, applied fairly, without fear or favor.
10722:
Miscegenation is a noun that refers to the mixing of people from different racial groups — specifically through marriage, romantic relationships, sexual relations, or having children together.

In its simplest form: if a person of one racial background and a person of a different racial background enter into a romantic or sexual relationship, or have children together, that was called miscegenation.
Why This Word Matters More Than Its Dictionary Definition

This is not a neutral, everyday word like "collaboration" or "mixture." It is a deeply loaded, historically charged term — and understanding why is just as important as knowing what it means.

The word was not coined by people who were indifferent to interracial relationships. It was created and weaponized by people who were opposed to them. The word was built from the start to describe something they believed was wrong, dangerous, or unnatural. So the word itself carries that baggage. Using it today, outside of a historical or academic context, would be considered offensive, or at the very least, tone-deaf.

The word rose to prominence primarily in 19th and 20th century America, though similar attitudes and laws existed in other parts of the world (such as apartheid-era South Africa, and colonial regimes in various countries).

In the United States, many states had what were called anti-miscegenation laws — laws that made it illegal for people of different races to marry or have sexual relations with each other. These laws were rooted in white supremacist ideology and the belief that racial groups should be kept "pure" and separate.

These laws targeted relationships primarily between:

  • Black and white Americans
  • But also, in various states, between white Americans and Asian Americans, Native Americans, and other groups

People who violated these laws could face criminal punishment — including prison time. Marriages that crossed racial lines were declared legally invalid. In some cases, couples were harassed, threatened, or subjected to violence.
The Landmark Turning Point: Loving v. Virginia (1967)

The most famous legal case connected to this word is Loving v. Virginia, decided by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1967. Richard Loving (a white man) and Mildred Jeter (a Black and Native American woman) were a married couple in Virginia. They were arrested in their own bedroom because their marriage violated Virginia's anti-miscegenation law.

The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that anti-miscegenation laws were unconstitutional — a violation of the 14th Amendment, which guarantees equal protection and due process under the law. This ruling struck down such laws across all U.S. states at once. The case is a landmark in American civil rights history.

It is important to understand that miscegenation as a concept was always tied to racist thinking. The anxiety behind the word came from a belief in racial hierarchy — the idea that some races were superior to others, and that mixing them was a form of degradation or corruption of the "superior" race.

This pseudoscientific and morally bankrupt ideology was used to justify:

  • Slavery
  • Segregation
  • Colonialism
  • Genocide in extreme cases

So when you encounter the word miscegenation, you are not just reading a clinical description of interracial relationships — you are reading a word that was a tool of oppression, used to police people's most intimate choices and to enforce racial hierarchies.
How the Word Is Used Today

You will almost never hear this word in casual, everyday conversation today. Its primary uses now are:

  1. Historical discussions — when talking about anti-miscegenation laws, the civil rights movement, or racial segregation.
  2. Academic or legal writing — scholars analyzing the history of race, law, and society.
  3. Racist rhetoric — unfortunately, the word is still sometimes used by white supremacists and other hate groups, where it retains its original intent as a term of disapproval.

The neutral, respectful, and modern terms for the same concept are:

  • Interracial relationship
  • Interracial marriage
  • Interracial couple

These terms describe the same reality — people of different racial backgrounds in a relationship — without the centuries of racist ideology packed into them.

AspectDetail
  • What it literally means: The mixing of different racial groups through relationships or reproduction.
  • Who used it and why: Primarily used by those who opposed interracial relationships, to label and criminalize them.
  • Its historical role: Central to racist laws (anti-miscegenation laws) that banned interracial marriage and sex in the U.S. and elsewhere.
  • Its legal end in the U.S.: Struck down by the Supreme Court in Loving v. Virginia (1967).
  • Its tone today: Offensive and outdated; associated with racism and white supremacy.
  • What to say instead: Interracial relationship, interracial marriage.

Understanding this word fully means understanding that language is never just language — sometimes a single word is a window into an entire history of power, prejudice, and the long, painful fight for human dignity.
10723:
Miscellaneous describes a group, collection, or set of things that are of many different kinds — things that are varied, mixed, and don't all belong to one single, neat category.

The key idea is: no single unifying theme. The things in a miscellaneous group are different from each other in nature, type, or purpose. They are lumped together not because they are alike, but precisely because they are unlike each other and don't fit neatly anywhere else.

One of the most important things to understand about "miscellaneous" is that it carries the feeling of "catch-all" — a label for things that resist clean classification.

Think of a kitchen drawer that holds a spare key, some rubber bands, a birthday candle, a dead battery, and a coin from a foreign country. None of these things belong together in any meaningful way. They aren't "cooking tools" or "stationery." They're just things — varied and unrelated. That drawer is a miscellaneous drawer.

This is why you often see "Miscellaneous" used as a folder name, a budget category, or a section in a list — it's the place for everything that doesn't have a better home.

• "She kept a box of miscellaneous items under her bed — old photographs, a broken watch, some foreign coins, and a few postcards."
  • "The accountant had a category called miscellaneous expenses for charges that didn't fit the standard budget headings."
  • "The workshop covered a miscellaneous range of topics: cooking, budgeting, first aid, and public speaking."
  • "He spent the afternoon doing miscellaneous tasks — fixing a leaky tap, replying to old emails, and organizing his bookshelf."

In each case, notice how the items mentioned are different from each other. That mix of unrelated things is what "miscellaneous" points to.

This is where many learners go wrong, so pay close attention:

1. It does not mean "unimportant."
People often use "miscellaneous" for minor leftovers, so it feels like a word for trivial things. But the word itself carries no such meaning. A miscellaneous collection can include highly important items. The word only describes the variety and mixed nature of things, not their value.

2. It does not mean "random."
"Random" suggests things chosen or arranged without any thought or pattern. "Miscellaneous" simply means of various kinds. A librarian might deliberately and thoughtfully gather a miscellaneous set of books on many subjects — that's organized and intentional, not random.

3. It does not mean "messy" or "disorganized."
A miscellaneous group of things can look messy, because the items don't share an obvious theme. But the word itself only describes the variety, not the physical state of disorder.
The two ways it typically applies

A. Describing a collection of things already mixed together:
Here, you're observing that a group contains many different types of things.

"The attic was full of miscellaneous objects from past decades."

B. Describing things that span a wide range of categories:
Here, you're noting that the subjects, topics, or types covered are wide and varied.

"The notebook contained miscellaneous thoughts — a dream, a recipe, a list of names, and a half-written poem."

When a writer or speaker uses "miscellaneous," they are often signaling one of two things:

  • "This is a mixed bag" — Don't expect everything here to be related. There's variety, possibly even surprising variety.
  • "This didn't fit elsewhere" — These items are grouped together by default, because no specific category claimed them.

Both feelings carry a slight sense of looseness or informality — a miscellaneous group is rarely a tightly curated, themed collection. But again, this is about classification, not quality or importance.

"Miscellaneous" is almost always used to describe groups or collections, not a single item. You wouldn't normally say "this is a miscellaneous object." Instead, you'd say "these are miscellaneous objects" or "a miscellaneous collection."

However, you can say something like "a miscellaneous assortment" or "miscellaneous work" — where the noun itself already implies a collection.

Miscellaneous = made up of many different, unrelated types of things; varied and mixed in nature; often used as a "catch-all" label for things that don't fit a single specific category.

It says nothing about importance, quality, disorder, or randomness. It simply says: these things are of many different kinds and don't belong to one neat group.
10724: A miscellany is a collection of various, different things — things that are mixed together and don't all belong to the same type or category. The single defining quality is variety. Whatever is in a miscellany, the items are diverse, assorted, and don't follow one strict theme.
Two main ways this word is used

In everyday language, a miscellany refers to any mixed collection of different kinds of things — objects, topics, ideas, or items — gathered together in one place, with no single unifying theme.

Imagine you're clearing out an old drawer. Inside you find a pen, a foreign coin, a birthday card from 2011, a dead battery, a tape measure, and a peppermint candy. That drawer holds a miscellany of items. Nothing connects them except the fact that they ended up in the same place. There's no order, no single category — just a diverse mix.

More examples of this use:

  • A museum display featuring a random assortment of artifacts from different time periods and cultures is a miscellany.
  • A conversation that jumps from cooking to politics to gossip to childhood memories covers a miscellany of topics.
  • An old trunk filled with letters, medals, photographs, and old coins holds a miscellany of keepsakes.

This is the older and more specific use of the word, and it appears quite often in books and academic contexts.

In literature, a miscellany refers to a book, magazine, or publication that brings together writings of different types — poems, essays, short stories, anecdotes, observations — often by different authors, on different subjects, with no single overarching theme tying them all together.

Picture an editor who collects contributions from fifty different writers. One writes a poem about the sea. Another writes a short essay on grief. A third contributes a humorous story about a dog. A fourth writes reflections on city life. None of these pieces are connected by a common subject. The editor publishes them all in one volume. That book is a literary miscellany.

Many famous historical collections of writing were called miscellanies. Publishers used this word on the cover specifically to signal to the reader: "Don't expect one theme or one type of writing — expect a rich variety."

The key nuance: What separates "miscellany" from just saying "collection" or "mix"?

The word "collection" is broad and neutral. You can have a collection of stamps (all stamps — one category). You can have a collection of jazz records (all jazz — one genre). A collection can be very uniform.

A miscellany, however, specifically emphasizes variety and difference. It implies the items inside are from different kinds, different types, different sources. If everything in the group is the same type of thing, you wouldn't call it a miscellany. The word carries a sense of deliberate (or accidental) mixing of unlike things.

Think of it on a spectrum:

  • A jar of red marbles → a collection, not a miscellany (all the same).
  • A jar of red, blue, green, yellow marbles → closer, but still all marbles.
  • A jar containing a marble, a coin, a button, a pebble, and a seashell → now that is a miscellany.

The variety has to cut across types, not just colors or sizes.

The plural is miscellanies.

"The library shelf held dozens of miscellanies — old publications stuffed with poems, recipes, travel accounts, and political commentary all jumbled together."
The adjective form you'll often see nearby

The adjective form of this word is miscellaneous, meaning "of various types; not belonging to one category." You've almost certainly seen this word before — the "Miscellaneous" folder on a computer, the "Misc." label on a receipt. That adjective describes the quality of being varied and mixed. The noun miscellany describes the thing itself — the actual collection that has that quality.

So:

  • The items in the drawer are miscellaneous (adjective — describing the items).
  • The contents of the drawer, taken together, form a miscellany (noun — naming the collection as a whole).

This is not a casual, everyday word. You won't often hear it in casual spoken conversation. It belongs to a slightly formal or literary register — the kind of word you'd find in books, essays, journalism, and careful writing. When a writer chooses miscellany over simpler alternatives like "mix" or "assortment," they're being precise and often a little elegant about it. It signals that the variety is notable — worth naming specifically.
Quick summary to lock it in

A miscellany is a collection of different, varied things — objects, topics, or writings — that don't all fit under one single category. In everyday use, it describes any mixed assortment of unlike things. In literary use, it describes a publication containing diverse writings of different types and authors. The heart of the word is always the same: genuine variety, all gathered in one place.
10725:
Mischance means bad luck, or an unfortunate event that happens by chance — not by anyone's fault, not by design, but simply because luck went the wrong way.

When something goes wrong and nobody is to blame — no mistake was made, no one was careless, the stars just didn't align — that is mischance.

This word works in two ways that are connected at the root:

1. Bad luck as a force or quality (abstract)

Here, mischance refers to the idea of ill fortune itself — the invisible, impersonal thing that makes events turn out badly for no particular reason.

"By mischance, he took the wrong road and missed the meeting entirely."

Nobody made an error. Nobody was irresponsible. It simply happened — that is the work of mischance.

2. A specific unfortunate incident (concrete)

Here, mischance refers to a particular event — a single unlucky episode that caused trouble or harm.

"A mischance on the mountain left the hikers stranded for the night."

In this sense, the word functions like "mishap" or "misfortune" — pointing to one bad event.

Both senses are correct and standard. Context tells you which one is meant.

The most common way you will encounter this word is in the phrase "by mischance," which simply means "as a result of bad luck" or "accidentally, due to chance."

"By mischance, she sent the email to the wrong person."
"The two enemies met by mischance at the same hotel."

It is a compact, elegant way of saying: this happened not because anyone intended it, but because luck was unkind.
What Makes Mischance Distinct From Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing where it ends and another begins.

Mischance vs. Mistake: A mistake involves a person making an error — a wrong decision, a failure of attention. Mischance involves no error at all. The person did everything right; luck simply failed them. A driver who crashes because they were texting made a mistake. A driver who crashes because a tire spontaneously blew out suffered a mischance.

Mischance vs. Mishap: These two are very close siblings. Both describe an unfortunate accidental event. The key difference is emphasis: mishap simply means a small accident or minor incident, while mischance places a stronger spotlight on the role of chance and bad luck as the cause. Mischance feels slightly more formal and literary than mishap.

Mischance vs. Misfortune: Misfortune is the broader, more general word for any bad situation or suffering — it can arise from bad luck, bad decisions, circumstances, or even other people's actions. Mischance is narrower: it specifically points to chance as the culprit. All mischance is misfortune, but not all misfortune is mischance.

Mischance vs. Accident: An accident is neutral in tone — it just means an unplanned event (a "happy accident" is possible). Mischance is always negative. It always involves something going badly by chance.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Mischance carries a tone of resignation and innocence. When a writer or speaker uses it, they are quietly communicating: "No one is at fault here. This was simply bad luck." There is a sense of helplessness to it — the universe did not cooperate, and that is all.

It is also a formal and literary word. You are far more likely to encounter it in classic literature, formal writing, legal language, or careful prose than in everyday conversation. In casual speech, people tend to say "bad luck," "a fluke," or "an accident" instead. But in writing, mischance adds elegance and precision.

To know this word completely, hold onto this:

Mischance = bad luck, or a specific event caused by bad luck, where no fault or intention is involved — only chance working against you.

If luck had been kinder, the event would not have happened. That gap — between what happened and what would have happened with neutral or good luck — is exactly where mischance lives.
10726:
Mischief is behavior, actions, or conduct that causes trouble, annoyance, or harm — but with a crucial twist: it almost always carries a sense of intentionality and often a dash of playfulness or cunning. The person causing mischief usually knows what they're doing. They're not being careless by accident; they're doing something deliberately naughty, disruptive, or harmful.

The word lives on a spectrum, from lighthearted naughtiness all the way to serious deliberate harm. Understanding this spectrum is the key to mastering this word.

At the lighter end — and this is the most common everyday use — mischief describes playful, naughty behavior that is a bit troublesome but not seriously harmful. Think of a child who sneaks up behind their friend and scares them, or hides their sibling's favorite toy, or draws on the wall when nobody's looking. Nobody gets truly hurt, but somebody is annoyed, embarrassed, or inconvenienced. This kind of mischief is often met with a mix of frustration and amusement. Adults looking back on childhood pranks often call them "harmless mischief."

In the middle of the spectrum, mischief describes deliberate troublemaking that is more disruptive and harder to laugh off — gossip spread to damage someone's reputation, lies told to create conflict between two people, or someone secretly undermining a plan. The intent to cause trouble is clear, and the effect is genuinely damaging, even if no physical harm is done.

At the more serious end, mischief means deliberate action intended to cause damage, injury, or loss. In formal and legal contexts, especially in British English, "mischief" can mean intentional damage to property. Here, the playful tone disappears entirely; the word is used coldly to describe wrongdoing.
Mischief as a quality or spirit

Mischief is not just an action — it can also describe a quality or spirit that you sense in a person or situation.

When someone says a person has "mischief in their eyes" or "a look of mischief," they mean that person has a playful, cunning gleam — a sparkle that tells you they're up to something naughty or teasing. You haven't caught them doing anything yet, but you know something is coming.

Similarly, when someone is described as "full of mischief," it means they have a personality that loves causing playful trouble, pulling pranks, or stirring things up. It's often said with affection.

These are the most common ways the word is used. Knowing them will let you understand and use mischief naturally in real conversations.

"Get into mischief" — to engage in naughty or troublesome behavior, especially when unsupervised. Parents say, "Don't let the kids get into mischief while we're gone." It implies the mischief is something that happens when nobody is watching.

"Make mischief" — to deliberately stir up trouble, usually between people. For example: "She made mischief by telling each of them what the other had said." This phrase strongly implies cunning and bad intent. The person making mischief wants to see conflict happen.

"Keep someone out of mischief" — to keep someone busy so they don't cause trouble. "Give him something to do — it'll keep him out of mischief." This is usually said about children or restless, troublesome people.

"A mischief-maker" — a person who regularly and deliberately causes trouble, spreads rumors, or stirs up conflict. Not a term of admiration.
How mischief differs from similar words

These distinctions are important because they sharpen your understanding of exactly what mischief means.

Mischief vs. accident: An accident is unintentional. Mischief is always intentional, or at least reckless. If a child knocks over a vase while running, that's an accident. If they push it over to see what happens, that's mischief.

Mischief vs. harm: "Harm" is a neutral, serious word for damage or injury. It has no playful connotation at all. Mischief can cause harm, but the word itself carries the suggestion of some degree of playfulness or cunning intent. Saying someone "caused harm" sounds clinical and grave. Saying they "caused mischief" suggests troublemaking with some element of naughtiness.

Mischief vs. prank: A prank is a specific act — one joke, one trick. Mischief is broader; it refers to a pattern of troublesome behavior or a general quality of troublemaking. A prank is a piece of mischief. You can say "that prank was pure mischief."

Mischief vs. misbehavior: Misbehavior is a general term for acting badly or against rules. Mischief is more specific — it implies troublemaking, annoyance, or harm done to others, often with cleverness or intent. All mischief is misbehavior, but not all misbehavior is mischief.

Mischief vs. malice: Malice means a deep desire to hurt someone badly. It's darker and more serious. Mischief, even at its most harmful, usually doesn't suggest the deep, cold hatred that "malice" does. Mischief can be serious, but it's rarely described as evil.

These sentences show the word across its range of meanings so you can see it in action:

  • "The two boys were always getting into mischief — hiding their teacher's chalk, rearranging the classroom, and blaming each other." — lighthearted naughtiness
  • "She watched the puppy with a smile, knowing that look in his eyes meant mischief was coming." — mischief as a quality or spirit
  • "He made mischief between the two friends by telling each of them that the other had spoken badly about them." — deliberate troublemaking
  • "The neighbors suspected the broken fence was not an accident but deliberate mischief." — intentional damage
  • "Keep yourself out of mischief while I'm away." — stay out of trouble
  • "There was a glint of mischief in her smile as she handed him the gift — he had no idea it was a prank." — playful cunning
The overall feeling of the word

If you had to capture the feeling of mischief in a single idea, it's this: deliberate troublemaking, ranging from lighthearted naughtiness to intentional harm, often with a sense of cunning or playfulness behind it. The lighter the mischief, the more we smile at it. The heavier it gets, the more we condemn it. But in all cases, it is never purely accidental — there is always someone choosing to cause trouble.
10727:
Mischievous describes someone who enjoys causing small troubles, playing tricks, or behaving in a naughty way — often for fun, and usually without serious intent to harm. Think of a child who hides their friend's shoes as a prank and then watches with a grin while the friend looks for them. That child is being mischievous.

The word carries a very specific feeling: there is enjoyment on the part of the person causing the trouble. A mischievous person is not sad, not angry, and not confused — they are having fun at someone else's mild expense, or bending the rules just to see what happens.

This word has a softer side and a sharper side, and understanding both is important.

The playful, lovable side is what most people mean when they use this word in everyday life. When you call a child, a puppy, or even a friend "mischievous," you almost always mean it with a sense of fondness or amusement. The trouble they cause is light — pranks, teasing, sneaky little games. Nobody is genuinely hurt. In fact, the person watching often finds it charming, even if they are mildly annoyed. A mischievous smile, a mischievous wink, a mischievous laugh — these all suggest someone who is up to something playful and knows it.

The sharper, more serious side is when mischievous behaviour actually causes real irritation, disruption, or damage — though still not in a deeply evil way. For example, someone who deliberately spreads a rumour to stir up conflict between two friends is being mischievous in a less charming, more harmful sense. The key idea here is still intentional trouble-making, but the consequences are bigger. Judges, newspapers, and formal writing often use the word this way — a mischievous lie, a mischievous allegation, a mischievous piece of reporting.

So the word lives on a spectrum: from harmless, lovable naughtiness on one end, to deliberate, disruptive trouble-making on the other. In casual, everyday conversation, it almost always leans toward the harmless, playful end.

Three things must generally be true for someone to be called mischievous.

First, the behaviour must be intentional. A child who accidentally spills juice is not mischievous — they are simply clumsy. But a child who sneaks the juice carton and pours it into someone's shoe while grinning? That is mischievous. There is awareness, a plan, and often a sense of delight.

Second, there must be a target or a consequence — someone is being teased, tricked, disturbed, or inconvenienced. Mischief does not happen in a vacuum. It involves someone doing something to a situation, a person, or a system of rules.

Third, the trouble caused is usually not catastrophic. The word would feel wrong if used to describe someone who commits a serious crime or causes genuine suffering. Mischievous sits in the space between completely harmless and seriously harmful.

Understanding what this word is not will sharpen your understanding of what it is.

Mischievous is not malicious. Malicious means wanting to cause real pain, deep harm, or suffering. A malicious person is driven by cruelty or hatred. A mischievous person is driven by fun, curiosity, or a cheeky desire to stir things up. The difference is in the intent. You can be mischievous and still be a good-hearted person. You cannot be malicious and still be considered good-hearted in that moment.

Mischievous is not accidental. Careless or clumsy people cause trouble without meaning to. Mischievous people cause it on purpose — and that is what gives the word its character.

Mischievous is not rebellious or defiant. Rebellious suggests a strong desire to fight against authority or a system. Mischievous is lighter than that — it is about tricks and naughtiness, not protest or resistance.

Mischievous is not innocent. An innocent person causes no trouble at all. A mischievous person causes some trouble, and they know it.
The Feeling and Tone the Word Carries

When someone is called mischievous, the word almost always carries a slight warmth to it, even when describing someone who is being a little troublesome. It is not an insult in the way "cruel" or "rude" would be. Calling someone mischievous is often a way of saying: "You are causing trouble, but I find you a little charming for it."

This is why the word is so often used for children and animals. A mischievous kitten knocking things off a shelf, a mischievous toddler hiding behind the curtain — there is affection wrapped around the word. Even when describing adults, a mischievous person is often someone who keeps life interesting, who bends the rules just enough to make you laugh (or sigh), and whose troublemaking is part of their personality rather than a sign of evil.

A mischievous look or expression is one of the most common uses of this word. When someone's eyes are twinkling, when they are suppressing a grin, when they look like they know something you don't — that is the look of a mischievous person about to do something naughty.
Can Things — Not Just People — Be Mischievous?

Yes. While the word most naturally describes people, it can also describe:

Actions and behaviours — a mischievous prank, a mischievous plan, mischievous behaviour.

Expressions and looks — a mischievous smile, a mischievous glint in someone's eye, a mischievous grin.

Information or communication — a mischievous rumour, a mischievous allegation, a mischievous piece of gossip. In this use, the suggestion is that the information was shared deliberately to cause trouble.

Animals — a mischievous puppy, a mischievous monkey. This use is affectionate and implies the animal is getting into things it should not.

Here are clear examples showing the word in use across different contexts:

"The mischievous boy put a frog in his sister's lunchbox and waited eagerly for her to open it."

"She gave him a mischievous smile before switching off the lights as a prank."

"The politician accused his opponents of making mischievous allegations with no basis in fact."

"There was a mischievous glint in the old man's eye whenever he told that particular story."

"The puppy had a mischievous habit of stealing socks and hiding them under the sofa."

"His mischievous sense of humour meant that no one was ever quite safe from his teasing."

Naughty — the most casual and simple synonym; often used for children; slightly less clever-sounding than mischievous.

Impish — suggests someone who is playfully naughty, like a little imp or fairy; very similar in tone to mischievous.

Roguish — a little more charming and adult; often used to describe someone whose troublemaking is attractive or witty.

Cheeky — means boldly playful in a disrespectful but lighthearted way; very close to mischievous in everyday use.

Wicked — when used informally, can mean mischievous (especially in British English: "You wicked thing!"), but in its serious sense it means something much darker.

Well-behaved — follows the rules; causes no trouble; does the expected thing.

Obedient — does what is asked; does not deviate for fun.

Innocent — not causing or intending any trouble whatsoever.

Serious — not prone to playfulness or pranks.

If you had to carry just one sentence about this word: A mischievous person deliberately causes small troubles or plays tricks, often for fun, with a knowing, playful spirit — not out of cruelty, but out of naughtiness.
10728:
A misconception is a belief that someone genuinely holds to be true, but which is actually false.

The critical thing to understand here is the word genuinely. A person with a misconception is not lying, not guessing, and not joking. They truly believe the thing they believe — they are just wrong about it.

Think of it this way: a misconception lives inside someone's mind as a "fact," but in reality, it is not a fact at all.

What separates a misconception from simply "being wrong" is that the person thinks they are right. They have no doubt. The false idea has settled in their mind as truth.

For example: For centuries, many people knew — with full confidence — that the Sun revolves around the Earth. They were not making it up. They were not uncertain. They sincerely believed it. That was a misconception.

This is why misconceptions can be so stubborn and hard to fix. You cannot simply tell someone "you're wrong" and expect it to click immediately. Their mind has already filed the false idea under "things that are true."

Misconceptions do not come from nowhere. They typically grow from one of these roots:

Incomplete information. Someone learns half the truth and fills in the rest with a wrong assumption. For example, a child learns that fish live in water, so they assume whales (which also live in water) must be fish. They later discover that whales are actually mammals — their original belief was a misconception.

Misunderstood information. Someone receives correct information but processes it incorrectly. A student hears that "the Great Wall of China can be seen from space." They misunderstand the scale of that claim, accept it, and carry the belief for years — not knowing it has actually been debunked by astronauts.

Inherited beliefs. Many misconceptions are simply passed down — from parents, friends, culture, or media — without anyone ever questioning them. The person never chose to believe the wrong thing; they just absorbed it from the world around them.

Oversimplification. Sometimes a complex truth gets boiled down so much that the simplified version becomes misleading. The simplified version spreads, and people believe the incomplete picture.

A misconception can belong to one person alone, or it can be shared by millions.

When a misconception is held by just one person — perhaps because of their own unique experience or limited exposure — it is simply their misconception.

But when a false belief spreads widely through a society, culture, or field of knowledge, it becomes a common misconception or a widespread misconception. These are particularly interesting because so many people believe the same wrong thing, which makes the false idea feel even more "obviously true" to any individual who holds it. The more people around you believe something, the more normal it feels to believe it yourself.

Some famous common misconceptions:

  • That we only use 10% of our brains. (False — we use virtually all of our brain.)
  • That lightning never strikes the same place twice. (False — it frequently does.)
  • That humans have only five senses. (False — we have many more, including balance, temperature, pain, and others.)

Here is something subtle but important: the word misconception is generally gentle and non-judgmental in tone.

When you tell someone they have a "misconception," you are not calling them stupid. You are acknowledging that their error is understandable — that it makes sense why they would think that, even though it happens to be wrong. The word carries a sense of "this is a reasonable mistake to make."

This is why teachers, doctors, scientists, and journalists often use this word. It allows them to correct wrong beliefs without making the other person feel embarrassed or attacked.

Understanding what a word does not mean is just as important as knowing what it does.

Not a lie. A lie is a deliberate falsehood — the person knows the truth and chooses to say something false. A misconception is never deliberate. The person believes what they are saying.

Not a guess. A guess is an attempt to answer something you are uncertain about. A misconception is a confident belief — the person is not guessing, they are convinced.

Not simply ignorance. Ignorance means you do not know something at all — there is a blank space in your knowledge. A misconception is more dangerous than ignorance because the blank space is filled in with something wrong. It is easier to teach someone who knows they don't know something, than to correct someone who already "knows" the wrong thing.

Not just an opinion. An opinion is a personal viewpoint on something subjective — like "I think this movie is boring." Opinions cannot really be right or wrong. A misconception, however, involves a factual matter — something that can be checked against reality.

Not a mistake. A mistake is usually an error in action or judgment in a specific situation — like making a mathematical error or forgetting to carry the one. A misconception is a false belief that can stick around for a long time, not a one-time slip.

Common patterns you will encounter:

  • "It is a common misconception that..." — the most classic sentence structure for introducing a false but widely held belief
  • "There is a widespread misconception about..."
  • "Let me clear up a misconception."
  • "She had a misconception about how the process works."
  • "He was operating under a misconception."
  • "This misconception has persisted for decades."

Common verbs used with this word:

ActionExample
clear up"Let's clear up a misconception."
correct"She corrected the misconception."
dispel"He tried to dispel the myth and misconception."
address"The article addressed a major misconception."
hold / have"Many people hold this misconception."
spread"The misconception spread quickly online."

Adjectives commonly paired with it: common, widespread, popular, dangerous, persistent, fundamental, basic

Misconceptions are not always about large, dramatic topics. They exist in every corner of life — in health, science, history, relationships, language, and everyday assumptions. In fact, most of us are walking around with at least a few misconceptions about something, without knowing it. That is not a flaw — it is simply part of being human and having limited access to all the world's information.

The moment a misconception is identified and corrected with accurate information, it stops being a misconception. The belief updates, and understanding replaces it.
A misconception is a false belief that a person sincerely holds to be true — often because of incomplete, misunderstood, or inherited information — and which requires correction with accurate facts.
10729:
Misconduct means behavior that is wrong, improper, or unacceptable — especially when it breaks an established rule, a professional standard, or a moral expectation. It is not just any bad behavior. The word carries the idea that the person knew (or should have known) what was right, yet they still acted in a way that violated that standard.

Think of it this way: if a child accidentally spills a glass of water, that is a mistake. But if an employee deliberately falsifies company records, that is misconduct — because it involves a violation of trust, duty, or rules that were clearly in place.
The key idea: a violation of expected standards

The heart of "misconduct" is this: there is a standard of behavior that a person is expected to follow, and they have failed to meet it — in a way that is serious enough to be considered wrong, not just careless.

That standard can come from:

  • A workplace's rules and policies
  • A profession's code of ethics (doctors, lawyers, teachers, police officers)
  • A legal system's laws
  • Widely accepted moral norms in society

When someone in any of these situations acts in a way that clearly crosses the line, their behavior can be called misconduct.
It does not always mean intentional wrongdoing

This is an important nuance. Misconduct does not always mean the person deliberately did something evil. It can range from:

  • Deliberate wrongdoing — an official who takes a bribe, knowing it is illegal
  • Gross neglect of duty — a doctor who ignores obvious patient safety procedures out of laziness
  • Abuse of power — a manager who uses their authority to bully or harass employees

However, a simple honest mistake — where someone tried their best and just got it wrong — is usually not called misconduct. The word implies some element of fault: the person was reckless, negligent beyond what is excusable, or deliberately wrong.

Because the word is used in many different areas of life, there are several well-known types:

1. Professional misconduct
This refers to behavior by a trained professional — a doctor, lawyer, accountant, police officer, teacher — that violates the ethical or legal standards of their profession. For example, a lawyer who uses a client's money for personal expenses is guilty of professional misconduct.

2. Gross misconduct
The word "gross" here means extreme or severe. Gross misconduct is behavior so serious that it fundamentally destroys the trust between an employer and an employee. Examples include theft from the workplace, violence against a colleague, or serious fraud. In most countries, gross misconduct can lead to immediate dismissal without any prior warning.

3. Sexual misconduct
This refers to any unwanted, inappropriate, or abusive behavior of a sexual nature. It can range from verbal harassment to assault. Sexual misconduct is taken very seriously in both workplaces and legal systems.

4. Academic misconduct
This refers to dishonest behavior in an academic setting — cheating on an exam, plagiarizing someone else's work, forging a teacher's signature, or bribing someone for grades. Schools and universities have strict rules against academic misconduct.

5. Official misconduct (or misconduct in office)
This applies to government officials, police officers, judges, or others who hold public power. When they abuse that power — for example, a police officer planting false evidence, or a politician taking bribes — this is called official misconduct or misconduct in office. It is a serious matter because these people are entrusted with public authority.

6. Willful misconduct
"Willful" means the person did it on purpose, with full awareness that it was wrong. Willful misconduct is considered more serious than negligent misconduct, because there was deliberate intent to act improperly.
The spectrum: from minor to severe

Misconduct is not always equally serious. It exists on a spectrum:

At the minor end, you might have an employee who consistently breaks a small workplace rule — say, repeatedly leaving early without permission. This is still misconduct, but it is relatively minor.

At the severe end, you have things like embezzlement (stealing money by falsifying records), sexual assault, or a public official deliberately abusing their power for personal gain. These are cases of serious or gross misconduct.

The consequence a person faces usually depends on where on this spectrum the misconduct falls.
How it is used in real sentences

Here are some examples showing how the word is used naturally:

  • "The nurse was dismissed from the hospital following an investigation into professional misconduct."
  • "Several students were expelled for academic misconduct after they were caught sharing exam answers."
  • "The committee found no evidence of financial misconduct in the organization."
  • "He filed a complaint against the officer, alleging police misconduct during his arrest."
  • "The company has a zero-tolerance policy on sexual misconduct in the workplace."
  • "Her misconduct during the hearing shocked everyone present."
How "misconduct" is different from similar words

Mistake: A mistake is accidental and unintentional. Misconduct implies some level of fault or wrongdoing — it is never a pure accident.

Misbehavior: Misbehavior is a more general, often informal word. It is usually used for lighter or everyday situations (a child misbehaving in class). Misconduct is more formal and more serious.

Crime: Not all misconduct is a crime. Some misconduct is handled internally — by a company, a professional body, or a school — without involving the police or courts. A crime, by definition, involves breaking the law and can lead to legal punishment. Misconduct can overlap with crime (like bribery), but they are not the same thing.

Negligence: Negligence means failing to take the care that a reasonable person would take, causing harm as a result. Negligence can be a form of misconduct, but misconduct is the broader category — it includes deliberate acts as well.

"Misconduct" is an important word because it signals that something more than just a poor outcome has occurred — it signals that someone is at fault. It is a word that appears in disciplinary proceedings, legal cases, news reports about institutional failures, and ethical reviews. When you see this word used, it is almost always pointing to a situation where accountability, consequences, or reform is being discussed.

In short: misconduct = improper behavior that violates a rule, duty, or ethical standard, for which a person can be held responsible.
